messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kai Tui, an American of Samoan and Niuean descent, was ten when the violence in his childhood home began to follow a predictable rhythm. He learned to recognize it by the sharp, acrid scent of singed cotton that sometimes drifted from the living room, a smell that arrived long before the shouting or the heavy footsteps. When that burnt odor filled the hallway, his body knew to brace, to shrink against the wall, to wait out the shaking. Over the years, he memorized the face that owned the house: a heavy brow, a sharp jawline, a particular way the eyes narrowed in the low light. Those features became a map he carried everywhere, so that years later, a stranger’s posture or the sweep of a familiar brow across a grocery aisle could instantly pull the past forward. He did not choose to remember; the memory simply arrived, unbidden and complete, dragging a white-hot surge of rage through his chest that made his hands tremble and his breath catch. When investigators or acquaintances asked him to describe what had happened, he would try to speak, but the words would dissolve in his mouth. He would lose the thread mid-sentence, unable to finish, and would instead step back, folding his shoulders inward and watching himself from a distance as if the events belonged to someone else. He started wearing only light, unstructured shirts, deliberately avoiding the heavy wool coats and dark denim that mirrored what the caregiver had worn. He stopped returning calls, stopped inviting anyone into his apartment, and told himself that keeping to himself was the only steady ground he had. His work as a detective placed him directly into the sensory landscape he had spent decades trying to outrun. Evidence bags at the precinct frequently carried the ghost of accelerants or smoke damage. Crime scenes smelled of burnt wiring, melted plastic, and charred wood. Each time he stepped onto a scene and that olfactory cue hit the air, his body reacted before his mind could catch up. His heart hammered against his ribs, his muscles locked into a permanent brace, and his eyes began scanning every room twice, watching every doorway, unable to let his guard down. At the same time, he made sure his own uniform and off-duty clothes never resembled the heavy, dark layers he had learned to fear. These physical reactions and his watchfulness ran alongside his marriage, neither folding into the other. The divorce papers arrived without a dramatic break, and Kai felt only a grim confirmation of his own suspicions. He looked at his own reactions—the missed shifts, the panic during roll call, the way his body stayed braced in calm rooms—and decided he was handling it poorly. He held onto the conviction that the violence had occurred because of who he was, a fundamental flaw in his character that made him vulnerable. He also came to believe that the world no longer operated on any predictable rules, that the foundation he had trusted had been completely stripped away. When people offered warmth or celebration, the feelings did not register as safety to him; they arrived as unfamiliar signals he could not decode, leaving him standing quietly while his nervous system remained locked in the past. Now, at fifty-six, Kai sat across from a clinician because the detachment had grown too heavy to carry alone. He could no longer afford to lose his train of thought during interviews, and the nights spent lying awake listening to his apartment settle, needing to stay alert for a threat that was not there, had left him moving through his days on fumes. He was looking for a way to quiet the constant watchfulness, to stop the rage from surging when the past broke through, and to understand how to exist in a world that no longer felt like it operated by any known rules. What he hoped for was simple: to stop bracing, to feel safe in his own skin, and to learn how to tell his story without losing himself in it.
